tldr: We propose HapticWorld, the world's first interactive world simulator that integrates real-time joint torque prediction and haptic rendering into a generative visual prediction simulator, allowing operators to collect demonstrations and evaluate policies while feeling physical feedback from the screen.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of HapticWorld. From the operator's commanded joint positions, it predicts visual latent representations while simultaneously reading out joint torques from intermediate features, rendering real-time haptic feedback back to the leader robot.
overview:
For robots to dexterously handle tasks involving object contact (such as opening doors or wiping a whiteboard), force/torque (F/T) information indicating "how much force is being applied" is essential alongside visual signals. However, gathering force-annotated data has been extremely difficult. Real-robot collection carries risks of damaging hardware or the environment and requires tedious manual resets. Physics simulators suffer from large modeling approximations (the Sim-to-Real gap), while recently emerged video-generation-based world models, though visually realistic, are vision-only and provide zero sense of physical touch.

To tackle this, the authors developed "HapticWorld," an interactive world simulator that accurately predicts the joint torques experienced by the robot alongside video predictions and immediately renders haptic feedback to the operator's hands. By reading out torques directly from the internal representations of the video prediction model, it closes the loop at 10 Hz without additional computational overhead, allowing humans to operate while feeling contacts in the virtual space.

Experiments evaluated three contact-critical tasks: opening a microwave door, wiping a whiteboard, and pivoting a box. With torque feedback, operators could intuitively gauge appropriate forces, raising demonstration collection throughput inside the simulator by an average of 1.6 times. Furthermore, when policies trained entirely on data generated inside HapticWorld were deployed on physical hardware, they succeeded in 54 out of 60 trials—approaching the upper bound of 56 out of 60 achieved with real-world data and far outperforming the vision-only baseline (19 out of 60). The authors also demonstrate that HapticWorld functions as a stand-alone platform for accurately evaluating force-conditioned policies.
contributions: Built the first interactive simulator that simultaneously predicts joint torques from internal features of a visual prediction world model and renders real-time haptic feedback to the operator's hands.
Showed that torque feedback improves operability within the virtual space, increasing demonstration collection throughput on contact-rich tasks by 1.6 times on average.

Demonstrated that policies trained solely on torque-annotated data generated inside HapticWorld achieve a high success rate on physical hardware (54/60 trials), rivaling models trained on real-world data.

Proved that HapticWorld serves as a stand-alone evaluation platform capable of predicting force-conditioned policy success rates with high correlation (within 3 trials of error) without using physical hardware.

sections.heading: Why world models need a sense of touch
sections.summary: Contact-rich tasks require force sensing, but real-robot data collection is costly, and conventional world simulators are vision-only without physical resistance. This paper presents HapticWorld, which predicts joint torques concurrently and feeds them back to the operator, closing the haptic loop between humans and generative models.
sections.details:
Mating parts, slipping grasped objects, pressing tools—in contact-rich manipulation tasks, "unseen forces" determine success or failure. Policies that observe force signals are known to significantly outperform vision-only policies, but training them demands large quantities of force-annotated demonstrations.

Collecting this data, however, is a major headache. Teleoperating on real robots involves exhausting manual resets after every run, accompanied by the persistent danger of equipment damage. Physics simulators (like rigid-body contact engines) avoid hardware wear, but their relaxed contact constraints and soft penalties introduce artificial artifacts that deviate systematically from real measurements. Meanwhile, interactive world simulators trained on real video (such as IWS) are realistic and safe, but strictly vision-only. As a result, operators feel nothing, leading to unrealistic motions like penetrating virtual objects that corrupt data, and the absence of force labels prevents training and evaluating force-conditioned policies.

To solve this, this work introduces "HapticWorld," which predicts joint torques in tandem with video generation and feeds them back in real time to the operator's hands via a leader robot. Without relying on physics engines or 3D object models, it learns entirely from prior play data to create a virtual environment equipped with both vision and touch.

sections.heading: At the intersection of video generation, haptic learning, and data collection
sections.summary: This section surveys three areas: world models, imitation learning with force/tactile feedback, and force data collection across real robots and simulators. The key novelty lies in closing the haptic feedback loop between a human and a learned world model for the first time.
sections.details:
### II-A World Models for Robot Manipulation
Recently, using video prediction models for robot learning and evaluation has attracted widespread interest. Progress has been made in fine-tuning pretrained models, planning in latent space, and serving as benchmark environments. The Interactive World Simulator (IWS), on which this work builds, operates interactively in real time on a single GPU; however, it remains purely visual and cannot handle forces or torques.

### II-B Force/Torque and Tactile-Aware Policy Learning
In contact tasks, policies that take force/tactile (F/T or tactile) inputs have achieved impressive results across multimodal fusion, compliance control, and recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. While these policies are the primary consumers of our system, they historically depended on physical sensor collection, running straight into data collection bottlenecks.

### II-C Force Data Collection: Real Robots vs. Simulators
To obtain force-annotated demonstrations, researchers have relied on real-robot methods like bilateral teleoperation (reflecting follower forces back to the leader) or physics simulators. Tactile world models predicting vision and touch together (such as ViTacWorld) have emerged recently, but they are limited to autonomous rollouts and lack a mechanism to render touch to human operators in real time to guide data collection itself. HapticWorld is the first system to achieve real-time haptic rendering with a human in the loop.

sections.heading: Reading torques from a visual model and feeling them in your hands
sections.summary: HapticWorld reads out joint torques from the intermediate features of a latent dynamics model trained on play data. By rendering gravity-compensated torques to the leader arm at 10 Hz, it closes the haptic loop between human and model without extra computational overhead.
sections.details:
### III-A System Overview
HapticWorld is built and used in two phases. In the first phase, unstructured "play data" (exploratory teleoperation without specific goals) is collected on physical hardware, recording camera images, commanded joint positions, and measured joint torques to train the model. In the second phase, operators collect successful task demonstrations within the trained model while feeling torques in real time, which are then used to train downstream policies.

### III-B Problem Formulation and Input Design
The model takes past RGB observations $o$ and operator commanded joint positions $a$ as inputs, targeting outputs of next-frame video $\hat{o}$ and robot joint torques $\hat{\tau}$. Crucially, the input action uses commanded positions ($a$) rather than measured positions. When the robot is in contact with a wall, the measured position stops, but the commanded position continues past the surface. Because contact force in a position controller is governed by this gap between commanded and measured values, feeding commanded positions resolves the visual and contact force ambiguity, making training effective.

### III-C Visual Prediction Backbone
The video generation module adopts a Consistency Model following IWS. Stage 1 trains an autoencoder to compress RGB images into 2D latent representations, and Stage 2 trains an action-conditioned 3D convolutional latent dynamics model $F_\psi$. This enables real-time autoregressive rollouts.

### III-D Reading Torques from the Dynamics Model
Instead of building a separate torque predictor, torques are read out directly from intermediate features $\Phi_t$ at the widest channel block of $F_\psi$ using a "torque head $h_\omega$" consisting of pooling and a lightweight MLP. Contact state estimation is already performed internally by the dynamics backbone to predict visual changes, so the model simply taps into it. This adds only 181k parameters (about 0.5% of the total), and backpropagating the torque prediction loss into the dynamics backbone encourages contact-aware internal representations.

### III-E Autoregressive Interaction and Haptic Rendering
At inference time, a single forward pass yields video and torque concurrently, introducing zero delay to the 10 Hz interactive loop. The predicted torque is stripped of its gravity term $g(q)$ based on the robot model, passed through a low-pass filter and limiter, and sent to actuate all 8 motors (including the gripper) of the leader device (OpenArm 1). Haptic feedback in the gripper allows the operator to intuitively feel whether a handle is securely grasped through their fingertips.

sections.heading: Thoroughly validating torque accuracy, collection speed, and real-world success
sections.summary: Evaluations across three contact-rich tasks confirm high torque accuracy, with errors within 3.5–4.8% of maximum torque. Haptic feedback boosted data collection throughput by 1.6x, and policies trained on synthetic data achieved a 54/60 success rate on the real robot.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Three tabletop tasks where contact determines success were selected:
- Microwave opening: Gripping the handle without slipping and pulling along the hinge's circular arc.
- Whiteboard wiping: Visuals make contact pressure hard to tell, requiring appropriate normal force on the eraser.
- Box pivoting: Tilting a box upright while maintaining normal force within the friction cone.
For each task, 500 play episodes (~20s each) were gathered to train the simulator, after which 50 demonstrations were collected inside the simulator to train ACT (Action Chunking with Transformer) policies.

### IV-B Torque Prediction Accuracy (Q1)
On unseen test episodes, torque prediction RMSE reached 0.26–0.38 N·m, representing a relative error of only 3.5–4.8% normalized by each joint's maximum torque. As shown in Figure F4, the predicted curves closely track sharp transitions in real measurements.

### IV-C Impact of Haptic Feedback on Data Collection (Q2)
The number of valid demonstrations collected in 10 minutes inside the simulator increased by 2.4x on whiteboard wiping and 1.6x overall when haptic feedback was enabled (Table I). Without touch, operators either failed due to insufficient pressure or pushed with unrealistic force that caused simulator rollouts to diverge; force feedback naturally kept inputs in the valid regime.

### IV-D Real-World Policy Success Rate (Q3)
When torque-conditioned policies trained on HapticWorld data were run on the physical robot, they succeeded in 54 out of 60 trials across all three tasks (microwave 19/20, whiteboard 19/20, box 16/20). This approaches the real-data upper bound (56/60) and far outperforms the vision-only baseline (19/60).

### IV-E Fidelity as a Stand-Alone Evaluation Platform (Q4)
Policy evaluation scores measured inside HapticWorld matched real-world trial outcomes with high fidelity (differing by at most 3 trials out of 20). Vision-only simulators cannot evaluate force-conditioned policies due to missing force signals, whereas HapticWorld serves as an accurate, hardware-free stand-alone evaluation environment.

### IV-F Qualitative Evaluation on Additional Tasks
In pushing/pulling kettlebells of varying weights (5, 10, 15 lbs) and pulling and releasing a slingshot, operators reported that weight differences and elastic tension were rendered faithfully to their hands.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future challenges: New horizons opened by the haptic loop
sections.summary: HapticWorld reads out torques from inside a video model and reflects them to the operator, enabling high-quality demonstration collection and evaluation. Key future challenges include handling fast transient impacts and removing the need for per-task retraining.
sections.details:
This work proposed HapticWorld, the first interactive simulator to close the haptic loop between a human operator and a learned world model. By efficiently tapping intermediate features for torque readout, it achieves higher data collection efficiency, policy quality approaching real-world data, and faithful hardware-free policy evaluation.

However, the authors point out several limitations:
- Due to the 10 Hz control loop, high-frequency transients such as sharp collision impacts or sudden slip events cannot be crisply reproduced.
- Each task/scene requires its own play data collection and model training, meaning it is not yet a single generalist model.
- Because torque prediction is tied directly to the visual dynamics, visual artifacts or rollout failures immediately propagate as unnatural force sensations to the operator's hands.
Future directions include achieving faster contact response and building multi-task foundation world models.

takeaways: Intermediate representations of video generative models are already rich in contact dynamics, allowing accurate joint torque readouts with just a 0.5% parameter overhead.
Haptic feedback during simulator demonstration collection prevents operator under- or over-pressing, dramatically boosting both throughput and data quality.
Policies for contact-rich manipulation can be trained from scratch using only synthetic visual and torque data generated inside a world model, matching real-data performance.
A world simulator that outputs force observations acts as a powerful benchmark platform, allowing force-conditioned policies to be evaluated prior to real-world deployment.
limitations: The 10 Hz update rate cannot faithfully reproduce or render high-frequency contact transients such as sharp impacts or sudden slipping.
Requires collecting roughly 500 play episodes and 2 days of model training per task/environment, offering no zero-shot generalizability across unseen scenes.
Torque prediction relies directly on the visual dynamics model, meaning any visual degradation or hallucination causes distorted force feedback to the operator.
